passage: So this is awkward. I'm Pankaj, and last week I saw Elizabeth, my closest friend since Class Six, copy answers from the girl in front, who kept her paper tilted, during the unit test. I didn't say anything then. That night I sat on the terrace and made a list, actually counted it on my fingers: friendship, fairness to the others who studied, and my own integrity. My little sister, who calls me Bhaiya Judge, asked what I was doing. Here's what I noticed. Every finger matters and they pull in different directions. If I stay silent I keep the friendship, but I'm okay with unfairness, and I don't like who that makes me. If I speak up I protect fairness, but Elizabeth may never forgive me. It isn't a trick question. It's a real conflict. I haven't decided yet, but now I know what I'm choosing between.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try before deciding to report?
qa.a: Pankaj could talk to Elizabeth privately or ask a trusted adult for advice, since that may deal with the problem while respecting both friendship and fairness.

qa.q: How might the girl in front see the copying, if she knew?
qa.a: She might feel angry or betrayed that her answers were used without her knowing, and she would want the test to be fair.

I'm Jatin, and Sachin and I share a room at his parents' place while my family is in Dubai. On Tuesday night he sat at the desk with a sheet of paper, not studying.
He'd drawn three columns. When I asked, he said, “I saw Irfan copy in the chemistry test today. From a paper in his sleeve.” Irfan has been his best friend since Class Two.
He talked it through out loud, maybe more to himself than to me. “Column one: Irfan. He's my friend, and if I tell, maybe that's over. Column two: everyone else. Farida studied all weekend and might get fewer marks than him. That's not fair to her. Column three: me. If I say nothing, am I okay with that?”
He tapped the pen. “Every column is true. That's the problem. It's not simple.”
I didn't know what to say. He didn't decide that night. But he didn't pretend it was easy, either.

qa.q: Where did Irfan have the paper he copied from?
How did Sachin seem to feel while weighing the three columns?
qa.a: Sachin seemed torn and troubled, finding every column true and the choice anything but simple.

qa.q: What could Sachin do next to move toward a decision?
qa.a: Talk to Irfan privately first, or describe it to a parent without names, before deciding whether a teacher needs to know.

qa.q: How might Farida be affected if nothing is said?
qa.a: Farida, who studied all weekend, might end up with fewer marks than someone who copied, which is unfair to her.

grounding: A cousin watches a student who saw his close friend copy list friendship, fairness to others and his own integrity, and see that the conflict is real.

Wednesday: At lunch he sits with Lakshmi as usual and says nothing about it. The words are right there. He talks about cricket instead and hates it a little.
Friday: The marks come out. Lakshmi scored higher than most of the class. Vikas looks at his list again and underlines one line: this is real, not simple. He decides he will at least talk to her before the weekend.

qa.a: Starting gently, saying what he saw and that it worries him, and asking why, so it feels like care rather than accusation.

qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt a jolt of fear and embarrassment, knowing her friend had seen.
